thread.title: Small-Cap Stocks Are Lagging. Here's Why and What Comes Next

title: Small-Cap Stocks Are Lagging. Here's Why and What Comes Next
text:
Small-Cap Stocks Are Lagging. Here’s Why and What Comes Next Nicholas Jasinski Oct. 8, 2018 5:00 a.m. ET Order Reprints Hulton Archive/Getty Images Text size
Small-cap stocks were all the rage for most of 2018, especially as trade fears weighed on larger cap multinational stocks. Heading into September, the small-cap focused Russell 2000 index was up 13.4% versus 8.5% for the large-cap S&P 500.
But the small-cap trade suddenly began to lag in September. The Russell 2000 index fell 2.4% last month, compared to a 0.6% gain for the S&P 500 and a 2.0% lift for the Dow Jones Industrial Average. The S&P SmallCap 600 was down 3.3% on the month.
Such divergence between big and small companies is rare, according to S&P Global’s Jodie Gunzberg. Since 1994, the S&P SmallCap 600 fell in only 8.1% of months in which the S&P 500 rose.
The Russell 2000 includes 2,000 U.S. companies with a median market value of $964 million.
Investors piled into smaller and largely domestic companies in 2018 as several tailwinds made them more attractive than bigger global firms. A booming U.S. economy far outpaced sluggish economic growth abroad. Meanwhile, favorable tax legislation and easing regulation have led to strong earnings growth, benefiting small firms that don’t have the same resources as giants to lobby politicians and devote to legal and other compliance costs.
(Big tech stocks including Amazon.com (AMZN) and Apple (AAPL) powered the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite to a leading 17.5% gain in the first eight months of the year.)
Further boosting small-caps was the steadily strengthening U.S. dollar, hurting the foreign earnings of large firms when translated back to dollars. About 15% of Russell 2000 sales come from overseas, compared to over 40% for the S&P 500. According to Howard Lu, portfolio manager and director of research at small-cap investment firm First Wilshire, investing in small-caps is one way to bet on the U.S. economy versus the rest of the world.
“To the extent that the domestic economy is performing better than the international economy, whether it’s in reality or investors’ perception, that would favor the Russell 2000,” Lu told Barron’s. While small-caps were rallying, the MSCI All Country World Index excluding the U.S., fell 4.9%. That reversed last month as the Russell lost 2.4% and the all-country index grew 0.4%.
So why the turnaround in small-caps versus large? The steady stream of negative trade headlines eased slightly in September, according to Craig Hodges, portfolio manager of the Hodges Small Cap Fund. The latest round of tariffs between the U.S. and China had less of a tangible impact than some had predicted, a U.S.-South Korea trade pact was signed, and Nafta renegotiations progressed to a deal. As trade fears eased, some investors who had been most heavily weighted to domestic stocks began to rebalance their portfolios back to global names.
“It really paid off for the people who stayed domestic during the previous trade wars with the saber rattling and all the news headlines,” Hodges told Barron’s. Then, “you saw some profit taking ... out of small-caps and into international and some of the markets that had been hit so incredibly hard.”
Some reversion to the mean could be expected, Leuthold Group Chief Investment Strategist Jim Paulsen noted, with small-caps performing roughly in line with large-caps since the early 2000s. When one has outperformed the other, it tends to be followed by a period in which the other catches up.
“One thing that would work as a result that I would argue from this is that if large [caps] have done well for a while, buy small,” Paulsen told Barron’s. “If small has been good for a while buy large. And that’s been a really good approach for the last 15 years.”
Sure enough, the year-to-date performance of large- and small-caps now looks much more even: The Russell 2000 has grown 7.5% in 2018 while the Dow and S&P 500 are up 7.7% and 8.5%, respectively.
Using enterprise value to Ebitda (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization), small-caps now trade at just a 1.1% premium to large-caps. That compares with a historical premium of 14.1%, according to Barclays Research. The current parity may be justified as headwinds build for the market as a whole, and the Russell 2000 in particular.
Bill Barker, portfolio manager of the Motley Fool Small-Mid Cap Growth Fund, prefers asset-light small-cap businesses going forward, given rising interest rates and other costs. “You’ve got some small-caps with higher leverage, which [as interest rates increase] are going to see their costs go up,” Barker told Barron’s. “The other place where they are seeing some pressure on margins is the input costs of wages or transportation.”
Barker points to Grubhub (GRUB) and Teladoc Health (TDOC) as examples of small-cap, asset-light names that investors should consider. Newsletter Sign-up
These days, Paulsen is less interested in the small-cap versus large-cap question and more focused on the psychology driving markets. That’s what he sees driving a relative resurgence in familiar large-cap names, like Amazon and Netflix (NFLX).
“Because of how long this cycle has gone, and with rates going up, people are becoming more risk-averse,” Paulsen says. “So people move to the popular, performing names, and feel good in those, which in part reflects some of their anxiety.” Close Small-Cap Stocks Are Lagging.
